https://www.vindobona.org/article/rememb.text: Remembering Polish Victims of World War II in Austria: From a Dramatic Escape to Vienna’s Central Cemetery To mark the upcoming anniversary of the outbreak of World War II, several high-profile commemorative events were held in Austria in collaboration with the Polish Embassy in Vienna. The celebrations focused on honoring the memory of Polish forced laborers and soldiers, as well as on Poland and Austria’s joint commitment to fostering a vibrant European culture of remembrance. Back in August, Zenon Kosiniak-Kamysz, the Ambassador of the Republic of Poland to Austria, attended a memorial event in Aspang-Markt (Lower Austria). The event was held to honor the memory of the Polish forced laborers Stanisław Krasoń and Ludwik Michalski. On August 21, 1943, the two men undertook a sensational escape attempt: They stole a German Junkers Ju 88 bomber from the Wiener Neustadt military airfield in an effort to escape the Nazi regime. According to historical accounts, their intended destination was Sicily, which was already under Allied occupation. However, the plan ended in tragedy: just a few kilometers from the takeoff site, the aircraft crashed in the border region (near Neustift am Hartberg and Zöbern), and both men lost their lives. The bodies of the two forced laborers were buried anonymously at the Unteraspang parish cemetery at the time. It was only a few years ago that the Austrian Ministry of the Interior, in cooperation with the Polish Embassy and the state of Lower Austria, initiated a historical investigation. Through archaeological and anthropological examinations, the remains were identified. Since 2023, a commemorative plaque at the cemetery has served as a memorial to their fate. The event was attended by numerous representatives from politics and government agencies, including Stephan Mlczoch (Head of War and Victims’ Graves Care at the Ministry of the Interior), Member of the National Council Thomas Elian, the mayor of Aspang-Markt, Doris Faustmann, Deputy State Police Director Manfred Aichberger, as well as the Polish military attaché, Colonel Maciej Betke, and Minister Counselor Przemysław Gembiak. In his speech, Ambassador Kosiniak-Kamysz emphasized that remembering the past is a commitment to safeguarding peace, human dignity, and democracy. Commemoration of the 87th Anniversary of the Outbreak of War at Vienna’s Central Cemetery On September 1, 2026—the 87th anniversary of the German invasion of Poland and the start of World War II—diplomats, representatives of the Polish community, and youth organizations gathered at Vienna’s Central Cemetery. Wreaths were laid at the monument to Polish soldiers and victims of fascism to honor the Polish men and women who fought against the Nazi regime of terror and gave their lives. In addition to representatives of the Polish Embassy, the ceremony was attended by the Association of Piłsudski Followers (Vienna “Danube” Group), scouts from the ZHP “Gniazdo” group in Austria, and numerous members of the Polish community. Inventor of the Legendary Marching Compass Honored A special focus of the commemoration at the Central Cemetery was Colonel Jan Bezard (Johann Ritter von Bézard, 1871–1954). Bezard was not only a prominent officer and military topographer but also the inventor of the famous Bézard compass. Born in what was then Galicia, the officer developed the marching compass—patented in 1902—during his time as a teacher. Thanks to its innovative bearing mechanism, the model served as the global standard for military and orienteering use for decades. Bezard died in 1954 in Vienna, where his grave of honor is located. Participants in the ceremony laid flowers at his resting place to honor his service to Poland and to science. Polish Embassy Vienna

https://www.dw.com/en/yemeni-leader-call.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5NJrw The civil war between the Saudi-backed Yemeni government and the Iran-backed Houthis has escalated sharply amid the Iran war Image: Marwan Abdullah Yahya Saeed Al-shabi/Anadolu/IMAGO Advertisement Rashad al-Alimi, the head of Yemen 's Saudi-backed Presidential Leadership Council, on Friday called for a general mobilization in the war-torn country. "I call upon the sons of our great people to engage in general mobilization and national mobilization, to rally around their armed and security forces," al-Alimi, who is also Supreme Commander of the Yemeni Armed Forces, said in a televised address. The head of the governing body urged his compatriots to join the government forces weeks after Yemen's government was dealt a major blow by the Iran-backed Houthi rebels . The Houthis have seized control of Yemen's entire Red Sea coast in a lightning offensive, allowing them to fully control the strategic Bab al-Mandab Strait, igniting global fears about shipping through the chokepoint. What else did Yemen's leader say? In his address, al-Alimi also said that the objective of the mobilization is to "restore state institutions and extend sovereignty over the entire national territory," including the Yemeni capital of Sanaa, which has been under Houthi control since 2014. He added that anyone who defects from the Houthis to the government will be pardoned in an upcoming amnesty. Al-Alimi addressed residents of Houthi-controlled areas , urging them to protect their children and not send them to fight alongside the Houthis. "The state does not view you as a party to the conflict but as its people and partners," he said. Why can't Saudi Arabia stop the Houthis? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Houthis escalate conflict For more than a decade, the Houthis have been fighting Yemen's Saudi-backed government. Although a 2022 truce left the conflict largely frozen, fighting has recently flared up again amid the wider conflict involving Iran. In recent weeks, the Houthis have intensified their missile and drone attacks on neighboring Saudi Arabia. They declared a maritime blockade and attacked Saudi targets in an attempt to stifle Saudi oil exports. The Houthis accuse the kingdom of besieging Yemeni areas under their control. They attacked Riyadh for the first time in years over the weekend , marking a major escalation. Edited by: Rana Taha Don't let the algorithm hide the news. https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/04/has-.text: Residents of Russia's Irkutsk region are deeply worried by rumours of a possible outbreak of pneumonic plague in this Siberian area. Speculation began to spread rapidly after the death of an employee of the Irkutsk Research Anti-Plague Institute.Darya Shipilova died in the early hours of 2 October in the intensive care unit of the district hospital in the town of Shelekhov. According to local media, she broke a test tube containing the plague pathogen.The incident prompted authorities to introduce quarantine measures: around 200 people have been placed under strict medical observation. The outlet "Baikal People" (source in Russian) reports that several Irkutsk hospitals were immediately closed and placed under quarantine, due to last three weeks. On Saturday, masks were made compulsory as a preventive measure at the Irkutsk aluminium plant in Shelekhov.Residents of Shelekhov have seen people on the streets wearing protective suits, masks and gloves. Local parents also say masks were handed out in kindergartens.Where did the plague come from?The deceased, a 28-year-old laboratory assistant, specialised in research on dangerous pathogens. According to the main account reported by her colleagues and independent media, on 25 September, while working with live biological material in the laboratory, she accidentally smashed a test tube containing the dangerous bacterium Yersinia pestis.Two days later Shipilova's condition suddenly worsened. She was rushed to Shelekhov district hospital. At first doctors, unaware of what had happened, suspected a severe case of coronavirus and admitted her to a specialised Covid unit. However, the rapid deterioration and the clinical picture forced them to carry out rapid tests for highly dangerous infections. The patient was put on a ventilator, but her life could not be saved.The pulmonary form of plague develops extremely fast and, without prompt and targeted antibiotic treatment, is almost invariably fatal.Are the authorities hiding information?The authorities' immediate response underlined how serious the situation was. The head of Rospotrebnadzor, Anna Popova, urgently arrived at Shelekhov hospital and took part in an emergency meeting of the sanitary and anti-epidemic commission chaired by regional governor Igor Kobzev.After the incident, officials initially restricted the information they released. During the first 24 hours, authorities in the Irkutsk region and Governor Igor Kobzev avoided using the word "plague". On 2 October Kobzev spoke of "a particularly dangerous infection" and said that "the situation is under strict control". The next day the authorities in Baikalsk urged residents not to travel to Shelekhov because of plague, but deleted the post a few hours later.The head of Buryatia, Alexey Tsydenov, also commented on the situation. Citing Rospotrebnadzor and the republican government, he said the woman's death was linked to plague infection, but later his statement was amended to a more cautious wording.This lack of clarity has fuelled panic on social networks in Irkutsk and neighbouring regions.Well-known Russian epidemiologist Gennady Onishchenko tried to reassure local residents, saying that plague carriers - rodents and fleas - in Siberia usually go into winter dormancy by early October. But that did not dispel people's fears."Pneumonia of unknown aetiology"On Sunday, Rospotrebnadzor said that the sanitary and epidemiological situation in Irkutsk region was stable, and that the woman had died from "pneumonia of unknown aetiology". The agency insists that further testing of samples taken from the patient did not reveal any micro-organisms related to her professional work."The sanitary and epidemiological situation in Irkutsk region, in the cities of Irkutsk and Shelekhov, is stable," the press service of Rospotrebnadzor said. "A special package of measures has been organised and carried out in connection with the illness of an employee of the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East, diagnosis: 'Pneumonia of unknown aetiology'."Rospotrebnadzor also stated that no incidents involving pathogenic microorganisms had been recorded at the institute and that "no staff member has sought medical help for infectious diseases in the past 10 days".

Photograph: Elizabeth Frantz/Reuters US Congress Congressional Democrats demand answers over ICE treatment of hunger strikers Immigrants at Texas detention facility, protesting against harsh conditions, say they face threats of force-feeding José Olivares Fri 30 Oct 2026 07.00 EDT Last modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 07.24 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Members of Congress sent a scathing letter to federal immigration officials this week demanding answers about conditions inside a Texas immigration jail, as detained immigrants on a prolonged hunger strike claim officials are retaliating against them and threatening them with force-feeding. A group of seven congressional Democrats sent the letter earlier this week to Markwayne Mullin, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) secretary, and David Venturella, the Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) acting director, protesting about the treatment of hunger strikers. The El Valle detention facility in Raymondville, Texas, detaining men and women, has fallen under scrutiny in recent weeks for allegations of harsh conditions. Detained immigrants on hunger strike say the facility has substandard medical care, undrinkable water and guards that mistreat them. Some hunger strikers are also protesting against their prolonged detention and are asking for their cases to move more quickly or to be transferred closer to loved ones in other parts of the country. “It is abundantly clear that DHS continues to demonstrate gross disregard for the health, dignity, personhood, and safety of our communities,” the group of lawmakers, led by the Illinois representative Delia Ramirez, said in their letter to the DHS and ICE. “However, we remain committed to conducting oversight, advocating for our constituents, and pursuing accountability.” The representatives “unequivocally condemn” conditions reported at the facility. “Whether they arose through indifference or inability, such conditions violate the … DHS and ... ICE documented detention standards,” the letter said. ‘What they’re doing qualifies as torture’: new details of ICE force-feeding revealed Read more “It’s clear that DHS continues to demonstrate gross disregard for our health, dignity, personhood, and the safety of our communities,” Ramirez posted on X . The congressional letter comes as the number of people detained by ICE increases amid the Trump administration’s aggressive but quieter anti-immigrant crackdown. In past weeks, senators from Georgia have similarly expressed concern about an ongoing hunger strike at the Folkston ICE detention center complex in their state. The Guardian reported last week that a man detained there died, even as allegations surfaced of force-feeding threats. The DHS denies the hunger strikers in Georgia have been threatened. The latest letter, signed by Representatives Ramirez, Texas’s Greg Casar and Jasmine Crockett and others, also demands details about the detainee population, the quality of medical care and more. “People should not be detained in these horrific detention centers – the hunger strikers should be released to their families and we demand that they receive protection from further detention and deportation,” the representatives wrote. “We also demand that you refrain from force-feeding any person in your custody.” In a statement, a DHS spokesperson said that the department responds to official correspondence through official channels and added that the representatives “should be thanking our law enforcement for removing these dangerous criminals from their districts – NOT vilifying law enforcement”. The DHS did not provide proof that the detainees participating in the strike, whose relatives spoke with the Guardian, have any criminal history. El Valle is owned by the Willacy County Local Government Corporation and operated by the private prison company Management and Training Corporation (MTC). The local government corporation did not respond to a request for comment. MTC referred all questions to ICE. The Guardian spoke with three relatives of asylum seekers detained in El Valle, who have all been detained for nearly a year and are participating in the strike, which is approaching three weeks. On 11 October, detained immigrants inside the El Valle facility launched the hunger strike. More than two dozen immigrants, from Russia, Cameroon and other countries, first participated, according to family members and advocates. There are now four women and 10 to 20 men still participating in the strike, family members said. One of the hunger strikers is Inna Eremeeva, an asylum seeker from Russia. While in detention, “she started having serious pain in her legs and her hips”, Eremeeva’s husband, Alexei, said through an interpreter. “She feels a growth in her private areas. She has been declined any medical care to figure out what is going on.” Alexei also said that officials earlier told hunger-striking women they would be transferred to another ICE facility to be force-fed. Other ICE detention centers in Texas have been used to force-feed detainees. In a statement, an ICE spokesperson said that “allegations that detainees are being threatened are FALSE. No detainees are being force fed or threatened with force feeding. “During hunger strikes, ICE continues to provide three meals a day, delivered to the detained alien’s room, and an adequate supply of drinking water or other beverages,” ICE added. “ICE is committed to ensuring the safety, security, and well-being of all individuals in its custody.” Eremeeva arrived in the US in 2024 and requested asylum. In November 2025, during one of Eremeeva’s work trips as a truck driver, she was stopped at a border patrol checkpoint in Texas and arrested by officials. She has been in detention since. The DHS said in a statement that Eremeeva entered the US “using the disastrous Biden administration CBP One app ”, which was used to process asylum seekers and “released in the country completely unvetted”. Eremeeva remains in detention as she challenges ICE’s attempts to deport her. “People are feeling hopeless and desperate in the black hole of ICE detention,” said Savannah Kumar, a staff attorney at the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) of Texas. “People in immigration detention centers across the country have had to resort to hunger strikes because they are caged in conditions that feel unsurvivable.” Amaliia Gilmutdinova’s husband , Shokhrukh Abdullaev, is also detained and participating in the strike. Abdullaev also worked as a truck driver and was arrested in November 2025 at a checkpoint in Texas. He entered the country in September 2021 using the CBP One app, the DHS said. “He is very afraid to say anything,” Gilmutdinova said about her husband through an interpreter. “He is very much afraid of being put back in isolation.” Another man, whose daughter requested their names not be shared for fear of retaliation, is 63 years old and struggles with various health problems. He is participating in the hunger strike. The man calls his daughter frequently with panic attacks and she guides him through breathing exercises to calm him down, she said. Kumar from the ACLU of Texas added that ICE “essentially locks people up away from their families indefinitely”, pointing to a recent fifth circuit court decision that ICE detainees in Texas, Louisiana and Mississippi do not have the right to seek release on bond. According to the 63-year-old man’s daughter, “the only thing he wants is to be able to see his family. He wants to be transferred. “He is like a child, asking: ‘Why am I here? I didn’t do anything’,” she added.
